results.title: Lunex Stealer Abuses AMD Driver to Disable Security Monitoring and Steal Browser Credentials
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
The Psychedelic Stealer malware distributed via compromised Ukrainian websites using ClickFix-style Cloudflare verification checks is part of a wider malware-as-a-service (MaaS) platform called Lunex.
The new findings come from Ontinue, which described the activity as a four-stage attack chain aimed at targeting Ukrainian-speaking users.
"The attack chain begins with a fake CAPTCHA page and culminates in the deployment of a fully-featured C2 agent," Ontinue threat researcher Rhys Downing said in a technical report. "The stealer extracts credentials and data from seven Chromium-based browsers, exfiltrates cryptocurrency wallets, and establishes persistent remote filesystem access through a PowerShell-based Native Messaging Host installed within the victim's browser."
The infection makes use of bogus MSI installers delivered via ClickFix to trigger a series of actions, including delivering a loader dubbed LunexLoader that's designed to bypass User Account Control (UAC) on Windows using the CMSTPLUA COM object, leverage the bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) attack for defense evasion, and finally download the stealer payload.
The use of the BYOVD technique is significant, not least because it's rarely employed as a precursor to a final-stage payload like an information stealer. Lunex takes advantage of a vulnerable kernel-mode driver for AMD Radeon Software ("PDFWKRNL.sys"), which is susceptible to CVE-2023-20598, to escalate privileges and blind security-related processes while keeping them running.
Psychedelic Stealer was first documented earlier this week by Arctic Wolf Labs, detailing the threat actor's modus operandi of compromising legitimate websites belonging to a hair-treatment clinic, a scale-model manufacturer, a specialist bookseller, a psychological facility, a tool retailer, and an automotive retailer to inject an iframe element designed to serve the ClickFix lure.
"Our analysis of the attack chain found that, before the stealer is delivered, the malware is designed to use a legitimate but vulnerable driver to switch off security tools on the victim's machine. With those protections disabled, the information stealer is then deployed to take browser passwords, session cookies, and cryptocurrency wallet data," Downing told The Hacker News.
The earliest reference to Lunex in cybersecurity literature dates back to June 2026, when BlueTeamCoolTeam's Luke Wilkinson identified six active Lunex Stealer's command-and-control (C2) panels across the U.S., Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, and Ukraine.
| LunexStealer (aka Psychedelic Stealer) C2 Panel \| Source: BlueTeamCoolTeam | 
It's worth noting that both Psychedelic Stealer and LunexStealer refer to the same component of the MaaS platform. "'Psychedelic' is the name of the malware file that runs on victims' devices, while Lunex is the underlying platform being sold to multiple criminal groups, which is the reason for the name 'Lunex' and 'LunexStealer,'" Downing explained.
Upon execution, LunexStealer communicates with the Lunex panel at 193.178.159[.]128 over HTTP to facilitate comprehensive information theft -
- Steal credentials from Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Brave, Yandex Browser, Opera, Opera GX, and Vivaldi.
- Enumerate five desktop cryptocurrency wallets, Bitcoin Core, Litecoin, Exodus, Atomic Wallet, and Electrum, and four browser extension wallets, MetaMask, MetaMask Legacy, OKX Wallet, and SafePal Wallet, and exfiltrate relevant data from them.
- Establish persistence using a Registry Run key, a hidden scheduled task named "psychedelicloveUtils," and register a Chrome native-messaging bridge or host (NMH) that allows the stealer to perform additional actions.
"The host is backed by a 13,200-byte PowerShell script embedded in the .rdata section that implements the Chrome Native Messaging protocol over standard input and output," Downing said. "The NMH operates within Chrome’s process context. It survives stealer binary deletion, system reboots, and browser restarts."
The PowerShell script supports six file system actions -
- list_drives, to enumerate all drive letters C through Z
- list_dir, to list directory contents with file sizes
- read_file, to read arbitrary files in 512 KB chunks and those up to 524 MB
- write, to write arbitrary data to any file path
- download, to download files from the system
- run, to execute arbitrary programs
What's more, LunexStealer injects a malicious Chrome extension by manipulating Chrome Secure Preferences and declares extensive permissions for cookies, history, bookmarks, tabs, storage, proxy, scripting, declarativeNetRequest, and all HTTP and HTTPS URLs. This grants the extension complete visibility and control over a victim's browser activity.
Analysis of the Lunex panel points to a Russian-speaking developer or development team, with 28 unique panels identified across 13 countries, marking a major expansion from June 2026. These panels are hosted in Russia, the U.S., the U.K., the Netherlands, France, Germany, Turkey, and Bangladesh.
"That growth in just a few months shows the platform is actively expanding and being used by either one threat actor or sold for other actors, not just a single operator," Downing said.
One of the panels hosted in Turkey has been found to resolve to five phishing domains -
- account-sams-club[.]com
- teamwork-recover-password[.]com
- namshi-uae[.]com
- whatsappbusineses[.]com
- ibraq-perfumes[.]com
This indicates that the MaaS platform's feature set extends beyond credential theft to also enable brand impersonation and phishing.
"The BYOVD delivery chain, using PDB-guided kernel callback zeroing rather than process termination, represents a quieter approach to EDR neutralisation that leaves security products running but blind," Ontinue said.
"Validated testing demonstrated that neither HVCI nor the current Microsoft Vulnerable Driver Blocklist prevents the specific PDFWKRNL.sys variant used in this chain from loading, a gap that persists despite the driver hash being catalogued in the LOLDrivers project since March 2026."
results.summary:
The Lunex malware-as-a-service platform is actively targeting Ukrainian users with the Psychedelic Stealer, utilizing sophisticated ClickFix lures and vulnerable drivers to bypass Windows security and exfiltrate data.

### Key Points
- The attack chain uses fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA pages and MSI installers to deploy the LunexLoader, which facilitates credential and cryptocurrency theft.
- Attackers exploit a vulnerable AMD Radeon driver (CVE-2023-20598) to disable security software while keeping processes running to avoid detection.
- The malware targets seven Chromium-based browsers and multiple desktop and extension-based cryptocurrency wallets to harvest sensitive user information.
- Persistence is maintained through Registry keys, scheduled tasks, and a PowerShell-based Native Messaging Host that survives system reboots.
- Researchers identified 28 active command-and-control panels across 13 countries, indicating a rapid expansion of the platform since June 2026.

### Why it Matters
This campaign demonstrates a significant evolution in malware-as-a-service operations by combining advanced kernel-level evasion with persistent browser-based data theft. The ability to bypass standard security blocklists highlights a critical vulnerability in how enterprise environments manage and validate third-party drivers.

results.title: From tunnel to connectivity layer: What GnuVPN says about where VPNs are heading
results.author: Will Jones
results.content:
For years, consumer VPNs were easy to explain: choose a server, create an encrypted tunnel, and route your traffic through it. The product category was built around a fairly simple idea, and the buying criteria followed the same logic, speed, server count, and price.
That description is becoming less complete.
The way people connect to the internet is now far more fragmented than it was when VPNs first became mainstream consumer software. A laptop may spend the morning on home Wi-Fi, the afternoon on a corporate network, and the evening tethered to a phone. A smartphone can move between Wi-Fi and cellular data repeatedly without the user thinking about it. Travel adds hotel networks, airports, roaming, and increasingly eSIMs.
The network keeps changing. The expectation that connectivity should remain private, usable, and largely invisible does not.
Connectivity has become the harder problem
This changes what users need from a VPN. Encryption still matters, but the practical question is no longer simply whether a tunnel can be created. It is whether that connection remains usable when the network around it changes.
That helps explain why protocol choice, once something largely left to technically minded users, is becoming more relevant. WireGuard has become a popular option partly because of its deliberately lean design and focus on performance. But different protocols can respond differently to network conditions, leaving room for alternatives when the obvious choice is not the most practical one.
The point is not that users should spend their day manually comparing protocols. Ideally, they should not have to think about them at all. Giving the software more than one way to establish a protected connection simply gives it more room to adapt.
GnuVPN is a useful example of that approach. The service supports several connection options, including WireGuard, OpenVPN, SoftEther, and AmneziaWG. WireGuard can serve as an everyday option, while the alternatives provide other ways to establish a connection when network conditions become less straightforward.
The same principle applies beyond protocols. A service intended to sit quietly in the background of everyday internet use also needs to work across the devices people actually use.
GnuVPN’s downloads page currently offers clients for Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, Ubuntu, and Debian. Android distribution also extends beyond Google Play to Huawei AppGallery and Xiaomi GetApps. That breadth matters less as a box-ticking exercise than as a reflection of how fragmented personal computing has become: one person may work on Windows, travel with an Android phone, and keep another machine on Linux.
Cross-platform support is therefore part of the same connectivity problem. The tool needs to remain available as the user moves between devices, not just networks.
When privacy tools meet connectivity tools
The more interesting shift starts one step earlier.
A traditional VPN assumes the user is already online. It protects a connection that already exists. An eSIM solves a different problem: getting the device onto a mobile network in the first place.
Technically, those are separate jobs. To someone landing in another country, the distinction matters much less. The immediate task is simply to get online without unnecessary roaming friction and then use that connection with privacy in mind.
That is why the growing overlap between VPNs and travel connectivity is worth watching. GnuVPN now offers eSIMSecure plans that combine mobile data with a VPN subscription, placing access and privacy in the same product flow rather than treating them as completely separate purchases.
The broader mobile market helps explain why that combination is becoming more plausible. According to the GSMA Intelligence 2025 Global Consumer Survey, 12% of consumers who had travelled internationally during the previous 12 months used an eSIM while abroad. More than 70% of those users obtained a travel eSIM from a mobile operator.
This does not mean every VPN will become an eSIM provider, or that the two products are interchangeable. It points to something simpler: the line between tools that provide connectivity and tools that protect it is becoming less rigid.
For VPN companies, that changes the competitive picture. Server count and benchmark speed still matter, but so do continuity across devices, resilience across different network environments, and ease of everyday use.
The VPN is becoming less visible
None of this means a VPN is becoming an all-purpose connectivity tool.
It cannot repair a poor mobile signal, guarantee access through every restrictive network, replace endpoint security, or prevent a website from recognizing a signed-in user. More protocols do not remove those limits, and adding an eSIM does not make mobile connectivity itself a privacy technology.
What is changing is how much of the surrounding experience a VPN is expected to handle.
The original consumer VPN flow was deliberately visible: open the app, choose a country, press Connect. Increasingly, the expectation is that the service should simply keep working as the user moves between devices and network environments, with fewer reasons to think about what is happening underneath.
Taken together, protocol flexibility, broad platform support, and travel connectivity point to a wider shift in the category. They are increasingly being treated as parts of the same product experience rather than separate technical features.
That may be a more useful way to think about where VPNs are heading. The next stage is likely to be less about adding another headline feature and more about making protected connectivity fit more naturally into the way people already get online.

results.summary:
Consumer VPN providers are evolving beyond basic encryption by integrating protocol flexibility, cross-platform support, and travel-focused eSIM services to maintain stable connectivity across increasingly fragmented network environments.

### Key Points
- Modern VPNs are shifting focus from simple server counts to network resilience, utilizing multiple protocols like WireGuard, OpenVPN, and AmneziaWG to maintain stable connections.
- Services like GnuVPN are expanding cross-platform compatibility to include Windows, macOS, Linux, and mobile app stores like Huawei AppGallery and Xiaomi GetApps.
- The integration of eSIM technology allows users to combine mobile data access with privacy tools, streamlining the experience for international travelers.
- According to the GSMA Intelligence 2025 Global Consumer Survey, 12% of international travelers utilized eSIMs, highlighting a growing market for integrated connectivity solutions.
- The industry is moving toward "invisible" security, where software automatically adapts to changing network conditions without requiring manual user intervention.

### Why it Matters
The convergence of connectivity and privacy tools reflects a fundamental shift in how consumers expect digital security to function in a mobile-first world. By bundling services like eSIMs with VPNs, providers are positioning themselves as essential infrastructure for seamless, secure internet access rather than just standalone privacy utilities.

results.title: We asked our Gen Z and millennial reporters and editors about AI agents. Here's where they split.
results.author: Martina Nacach Cowan Ros
results.content:
Everyone is talking about AI agents — and Business Insider's reporters and editors are no different.
Agents go a step beyond chatbots and are capable of planning and achieving multi-step tasks. This can range from making a restaurant reservation to inviting a friend for lunch to buying clothes you are on the lookout for.
To get a sense of how members of different generations feel about the emerging world of AI agents, I, a Gen Z fellow on the Business Insider Economy team, talked to my colleagues, spanning from Gen Z to elder millennials, about their stances on the divisive topic.
While the younger generation expressed a lot of worries around privacy, the millennials in the group were cautiously optimistic about how agents could be helpful at work and at home.
The Gen Z consensus: Skepticism and privacy concerns
Many of my Gen Z peers agreed that growing up with technology made them more aware of its limitations and dangers — making them more hesitant about handing over their information to AI agents. They also seemed most concerned about privacy and scams.
The younger members of the Economy team aren't alone — a recent poll from the Pew Research Center found that Americans under age 30 are increasingly skeptical of AI's benefits.
Ayelet Sheffey, our Gen Z senior education reporter, said she was not open to handing over the control to an AI agent to get things she needed done.
"I'm hearing about people using AI and they're like feeding their bank information or personal things into a software — that just immediately turns me off," she said. "Not only for the privacy reasons, but also, I just don't trust anyone or anything else to get tasks done."
Allie Kelly, a Gen Z economy reporter, said that while being a reporter is a public-facing job, there is other information she prefers to keep private. While she is open to using it for professional purposes, she is more hesitant to use it for personal reasons, not knowing how the information she provides to the agent can be used.
"If I want an agent to analyze something, I will give it something specific to analyze — I'm not going to give it access to my inbox," she said. "It's not just my information; sometimes it's sources' information, so I just want to be cognizant of that."
Juliana Kaplan, a Gen Z senior reporter, said she is wary of handing her personal information over to companies that could have different incentives influencing how their AI agents work. She posed a rhetorical question: If a company with an AI agent had a deal with a credit card company, and she was using an agent to choose her next credit card, would it be influenced to recommend that one?
"I would have to do a lot of research into the amount of due diligence they have done with my information," she said. "At that point, I'm like, I can just do it myself."
Noah Sheidlower, a Gen Z senior economy reporter, said, "I'm all for efficiency and maximizing time I could be spending on things that are meaningful to me, but I don't fully trust giving up my authority and agency to make decisions. I've read stories of agents invading privacy and doing tasks it should not be doing that have harmful repercussions, and I want to stay in control as much as I can until the agents are more advanced."
Madison Hoff, a Gen Z economy reporter, said that while she sees the value of agents in helping manage work, she enjoys working on things herself. When looking for craft ideas in her free time, she said she enjoys the process of looking around her and finding ideas — even if an AI agent would help her do it more quickly.
"I rather just use the brain power a little more and do the research," she said.
Several of the Gen Z reporters said that while friends in creative fields were more hesitant to adopt AI agents, peers in finance, consulting, and tech-adjacent fields seemed more open to adopting them earlier.
The millennial consensus: Cautious optimism
The idea that AI agents still have a long way to go before they are accurate and efficient enough was shared by the Economy team's millennial editors, who held a more cautious optimism about the future of adopting agents to streamline workflows and team operations.
Bartie Scott, a millennial and economy deputy editor, said that while she has environmental concerns about using AI, she does see potential in using it to reduce her screen time — especially with voice agents.
"As someone who has a job that's on a screen, it can feel insurmountable sometimes," she said. "We have so much to do in modern life that you feel burned out — And I think this, maybe in an ideal world, could be like a solution to that."
Scott said that while she is not an early adopter of technology, once she has seen people she respects say the technology is trustworthy and easy to use, she might be inclined to dabble in it. Examples she thought of would be if she could get an agent to help brief her on her workday priorities and daily check-ins.
"If I could do all that with voice commands, that would kind of be a dream," she said.
Andy Kiersz, a millennial and senior economic data editor, agreed that he might be more in the mid-adopter camp than the early-adopter camp. If a "sufficiently long period of time" passes with no major data breaches and a situation like planning a trip arises where it would be useful, he said he would consider using an agent.
Kiersz sees some potential for agentic AI at work. "I could totally see putting an agent to go crawl repositories of economics papers and read through the abstracts," he said. He sees himself sending agents to do the "tedious side of the job," so he can focus on the "interesting side of the job."
Two millennials on the team had the most hands-on experience with these new toys.
Ryan Kailath, an elder millennial and senior editor, is a "big pointsmaxxer," as a member of many airline loyalty programs. Yet, finding awards when booking is always a hefty logistical task. So Kailath used Muse, the personal AI agent launched by Meta in early September, to see what all the fuss was about and look into booking for an upcoming trip.
Although the AI agent took the lead, it encountered many problems that Kailath had to resolve manually, such as login credentials and two-factor authentication codes required to continue the search.
"My one test case where I thought, 'Here's a big friction in my life, maybe an agent could make this friction easier,' it failed miserably," he said. Yet, Kailath said that if it improved in the future, he would no doubt use it.
Our Senior Reporter, Jacob Zinkula, also had a brief 10-minute encounter with Muse. Zinkula, a young millennial, downloaded the app to see if it could help him get a future reservation at a high-demand restaurant for the Christmas season, but has yet to figure it out. Caught in the cusp of the Gen Z and millennial generations, he is more cautious about letting an AI agent make financial decisions on its own, but is open to waiting to see how they could develop and be useful in the future.
"I try to be open but skeptical," he said. "It doesn't feel like there's an immediate need for me to like jump onto it too soon. That said, I'm open to ways it could be helpful going forward. For better or worse, this stuff's probably not going away."
results.summary:
Business Insider reporters from Gen Z and millennial generations express differing levels of skepticism and optimism regarding the adoption of AI agents for personal and professional tasks.

### Key Points
- AI agents are designed to perform multi-step tasks like booking travel or managing schedules, moving beyond the capabilities of standard chatbots.
- Gen Z staff cited significant concerns regarding data privacy, potential scams, and the loss of personal agency when delegating tasks to automated software.
- Millennial editors expressed cautious optimism, viewing AI agents as potential tools to reduce screen time and automate tedious professional workflows.
- Practical testing of Meta’s Muse AI agent revealed current limitations, including failures with two-factor authentication and complex logistical tasks.
- Pew Research Center data indicates that Americans under age 30 are increasingly skeptical of the overall benefits provided by artificial intelligence.

### Why it Matters
The divide between generational attitudes highlights the significant trust barriers that developers must overcome to achieve widespread consumer adoption of agentic AI. As these tools evolve, their ability to balance efficiency with data security will determine whether they become essential productivity assistants or remain niche technologies.

results.title: The AI safety debate is confusing. Here's our guide to the different factions
results.author: Katie McQue
results.content:
The AI safety debate is confusing. Here's our guide to the different factions
The debate over the potential benefits and safety risks of accelerating artificial intelligence development reached a crescendo this month, as supporters and critics of the technology clashed over warnings that increasingly powerful AI could pose existential risks to humanity.
On September 8, Jacob Coxon, a researcher-turned-whistleblower, publicly resigned from major AI firm Anthropic after a previous stint at OpenAI, accusing the companies of "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
Coxon's claims supercharged an ongoing debate over the potential damage AI could wreak on society and prompted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and other AI CEOs to call for a slowdown in AI development.
Over the past two months, companies including OpenAI and Anthropic disclosed multiple incidents in which their AI agents accessed the internet when they weren't supposed to and carried out unapproved activities. In OpenAI's case, swarms of agents worked together to hack the open-source software platform Hugging Face and OpenAI itself, without alerting humans.
The debate over the safety of AI and whether and how it should be regulated is not a simple clash between two opposing sides. There are multiple factions with a variety of goals and assessments about the technology's promise, dangers and how it should be governed. Here are the main arguments shaping that debate.
Effective accelerationists and the tech right
Those who have an aggressively optimistic worldview of AI are often referred to as effective accelerationists (sometimes shortened to e/acc) – a term reflecting their belief that AI should be rapidly advanced.
People belonging to the faction are emphatically optimistic about AI and its future benefits to society. They believe that the technology can propel medical advancements, boost economic productivity, increase living standards, and automate dangerous or undesirable work. To achieve this, they argue that AI development should be accelerated, not restricted.
Effective accelerationists' ideology overlaps with that of the "tech right", in that both camps wholeheartedly believe in accelerating AI development and deployment and minimize critics' concerns over safety and security.
However, the tech right takes a more nationalistic stance, championing U.S. dominance in the global AI race. Like effective accelerationists, they believe that AI research and deployment should be unencumbered by regulation, arguing that could slow innovation or allow adversarial governments such as China to overtake the U.S. in the AI race.
The tech right's philosophy is represented by figures such as former White House AI and cryptocurrency advisor David Sacks, whose views remain influential with the Trump administration. Other significant players include venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman. The three founded the Leading the Future super PAC to support pro-AI political candidates, and campaign against those who advocate for regulation.
Andreessen also penned a 2023 widely-read blog post titled "Why AI Will Save the World," in which he claimed that fears of AI triggering mass unemployment are overstated. He argued that previous waves of automation ultimately created more jobs and economic activity than they eliminated, and the fears of existential risk are overblown.
Recently, Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, whose chips are used by most AI companies, has emerged as one of the industry's leading voices pushing back against calls for a slowdown and urging a light regulatory approach.
Populist right
AI has exposed an ideological split within President Trump's political coalition. While Trump and his advisers overwhelmingly favor accelerating AI, parts of his MAGA base believe the powerful corporations he has aligned himself with could undermine the U.S. economy.
Figures including former Trump strategist Steve Bannon and former Fox News host Tucker Carlson have been vocal about potential job losses, the tech industry's political power, child safety and threats to traditional social and religious values.
This month, Bannon formed an unlikely partnership with independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, a socialist, to call for significant restrictions on AI development, government oversight and corporate accountability at the Pro-Human Assembly conference in Washington, D.C.
Still, the two have differing stances on what any of those measures should look like. Sanders called for an immediate pause on AI development until clear safety rules are established by scientists, a permanent ban on the development of artificial "superintelligence" (AI systems that are more intelligent than humans in all domains), and an international treaty with China in an effort to avoid an AI arms race. Bannon, meanwhile, argued for slowing the pace of AI development, the formation of a national regulatory organization and for cutting off China from U.S. AI technology.
"So why are we letting the Chinese Communist Party drive us? Oh, we have to do this or China wins," said Bannon in his speech at the event in Washington. "We should quarantine now every aspect of the ecosystem of artificial intelligence away from the Chinese Communist Party today. We should cut them off."
Safetyists
Safetyists are primarily concerned with the potential risks of the rapid advancement of AI. Their worries center on the possibility of catastrophic or existential outcomes, such as the death of humanity at the hands of autonomous machines.
High-profile members of the safetyist community include Geoffrey Hinton, who is commonly referred to as the "Godfather of AI" because of his pioneering work in deep learning that helped launch the modern era of AI. In recent years, Hinton, who previously worked at Google, has issued a series of warnings about existential risks associated with AI, particularly if an AI model surpasses human intelligence and becomes autonomous.
Another vocal AI safetyist is Daniel Kokotajlo, a former researcher at OpenAI and co-author of AI 2027, a paper published last year that discusses how super-intelligent AI could lead to human extinction by the mid-2030s.
Effective altruists
Effective altruists (often shortened to "EA") generally believe in maximizing humanity's long-term welfare. The movement originally focused on material ways to reduce global poverty. But more recently, many EA thinkers have focused their concerns on the possibility of existential risks from advanced AI and other potential societal-scale disasters such as nuclear war, climate change and pandemics. They particularly worry about the consequences for future generations. People from the EA camp prioritize AI safety, alignment – which is the science of making sure AI systems behave in a way that is reflective of human values and in line with safety rules – and reducing the probability of catastrophic outcomes.
The key difference between EAs and safetyists is that EAs generally provide funding for AI safety research and risk mitigation, whereas safetyists are researchers and advocates undertaking AI safety work and publicly calling for regulation.
Other AI factions often derisively describe effective altruists as so-called "AI Doomers." EA has also become a focus of criticism from the Trump administration since Coxon's resignation from Anthropic.
"Americanism, not effective altruism. The United States will continue to be AI DOMINANT!" said one Defense Department post this month.
Well-known people in the EA movement include Eliezer Yudkowsky, co-founder of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), which focuses on mathematical approaches to making advanced AI systems safe. He is also the author of Harry Potter fan fiction that helped popularize ideas associated with EA. Holden Karnofsky, an American entrepreneur and philanthropist, founded Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), an organization that funds causes central to the EA mission, including AI and biosecurity. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is considered to be aligned with effective altruism. Karnofsky also works at Anthropic and is married to Daniela Amodei, who is a co-founder of Anthropic and the sister of Dario Amodei, the CEO.
Another high-profile supporter of the EA movement is Sam Bankman-Fried, who founded major cryptocurrency exchange FTX. In 2023, he was convicted of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy related to the misuse of customer and investor funds and is currently serving a 25-year prison sentence.
AI ethics
The AI ethics camp argues that society should focus on the harms AI is already causing, rather than on hypothetical existential risks. Some proponents contend that emphasizing existential threats from a hypothetical future superintelligence can serve as a distraction from the more immediate harms and accountability issues surrounding AI today.
AI ethicists' concerns include how AI systems can be biased due to the content of their training data, for example, the ways in which AI facial recognition or job application systems might perpetuate existing societal biases. They are also concerned with how AI could be used to exploit workers and to enable mass surveillance, as well as about the environmental costs of data centers, autonomous weapons, and the concentration of power among technology companies.
A notable voice of the AI ethics faction is Timnit Gebru, a computer scientist and former co-lead of Google's Ethical AI team. Gebru left the company in 2020 because of a dispute with the company over a research paper she wrote exposing problems with large language models (LLMs), including their tendency to generate harmful or misleading language.
AI as a normal technology
People belonging to the "AI as a Normal Technology" group reject both the utopian and dystopian narratives about AI. Instead, this faction sees AI as a powerful but ultimately normal technology, comparable to the internet or electricity. They believe the focus should be on understanding and regulating specific applications and harms instead of treating AI as an unprecedented threat or as a path to inevitable superintelligence.
Notable people associated with this worldview include Fei-Fei Li, a computer scientist and co-director of the Stanford Human-Centered AI Institute. Li is famous for creating ImageNet, a vastly large dataset of images which provided the training data for large neural networks, which led to several major developments in AI.
Katie McQue's reporting is supported by the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism, which is a grantee of Coefficient Giving. Neither Tarbell nor Coefficient have any editorial input into her work.
results.summary:
The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has triggered a complex global debate, dividing experts and policymakers into distinct factions regarding the technology's existential risks and potential societal benefits.

### Key Points
- Whistleblower Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing concerns that companies are recklessly racing toward self-improving superintelligence.
- "Effective accelerationists" and the "tech right" advocate for rapid development to ensure U.S. dominance and economic growth, opposing restrictive regulations.
- "Safetyists" and "effective altruists" prioritize long-term risk mitigation, fearing that autonomous AI systems could eventually pose existential threats to humanity.
- The "AI ethics" faction argues that current industry focus on hypothetical future risks distracts from immediate harms like algorithmic bias, surveillance, and labor exploitation.
- An "AI as a normal technology" group, including Stanford’s Fei-Fei Li, views AI as a tool comparable to electricity, favoring application-specific regulation over existential alarmism.
- Political figures like Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon have formed an unlikely coalition to demand government oversight and corporate accountability for AI development.

### Why it Matters
The fragmentation of the AI safety debate complicates efforts to establish a unified regulatory framework, leaving policymakers caught between competing visions of innovation and risk. This ideological divide directly influences corporate strategy, government funding priorities, and the future of international AI governance.

results.title: Enshittification Has a New Mascot, and He’s Teaming Up With Death in a Hilarious Ad Campaign
results.author: Joe Hindy
results.content:
Imagine, if you will, a pale figure of Death, dressed in a black robe holding a scythe, alongside a handsome, lumberjack-looking Nordic fella who goes by the name Enshittificator. As partners in crime, they conspire to make your life suck, all because they have the power to make digital products and services worse.
If that piques your interest — and maybe sounds too much like real life — a new “anti-enshittification” ad campaign is worth a few minutes of your time.
The term “enshittification” was popularized in 2022 by author and activist Cory Doctorow, and its massive cultural surge earned it a place in Merriam-Webster’s slang hub last year. Enshittification is a deliberate process, designed by companies to maximize profit.
More from CNET
It starts with luring you to a product or service, then making it so good that you become completely dependent on it. The next step is to pull the rug out from under you by hiding basic features behind a paywall, reducing overall quality and squeezing you for every last dime while providing as little value as possible.
The Death and Enshittificator video above, released on YouTube in mid-September, is the second of a series from the Norwegian Consumer Council, an independent, government-funded nonprofit that advocates for consumer rights. The main character, the Enshittificator, is a bearded Nordic man who says in the first video, released in February, that his “job is to make things shitty.”
The initial video concludes with Mr. Enshittificator getting into a car accident because he didn’t pay a subscription for his braking system, a scenario he appeared to find amusing. In the second video, he meets Death in the hospital, and the two enter into a business relationship. (He now dons a yellow hazmat suit to stay alive.)
The duo spends time making every conceivable product worse, from TVs and toothbrushes to smartphone storage. They point out that products with long lifespans, like the famously indestructible Nokia 3310 — which makes a cameo appearance — only generate revenue once. If companies want a profitable business model, however, they have to use low-quality materials, ensure products can’t be fixed and stop issuing updates.
“Look at all the companies that used to make solid products,” the Enshittificator said. “Where are they now?”
“Dead,” Death said, and they share a knowing smile.
The Norwegian Consumer Council’s ads are part of its Breaking Free initiative, a multipronged policy approach to make technology work in favor of consumers, rather than against them. The campaign craftily relies on dark humor to detail how enshittification affects everyday life, from paid subscription models to planned obsolescence, which forces you to buy newer devices.
The videos are also a strikingly accurate commentary on the dismal state of products and gadgets in the digital age. Prices go up while reliability plummets. Companies rely on shady advertising tactics and dodge consumer protection rights.
Doctorow himself collaborated with the nonprofit to help launch the series, which he’s immensely pleased with. In an email to CNET, he said, “The idea that firms’ market power means that they can worsen their offerings with impunity, combined with the minor license to vulgarity of my dirty little word, have proven a winning combination for helping people direct their anger in the right direction.”
Real life (and death)
The enshittification process is relatable and real. In 2020, Apple agreed to pay up to $500 million to settle the landmark “batterygate” class action lawsuit over allegations that it secretly slowed down older iPhone models through software updates. Powerful tech companies have poured massive amounts of money into lobbying against right-to-repair laws, preventing customers from fixing their own devices when they break.
“It’s really important that the products can’t be fixed,” said the Enshittificator. “It breaks, then it dies, so you have to buy a new one. And another one. And another one. And another one. And another one.”
“This way, we’re actually slowly killing the planet as well,” a smiling Death said, helpfully chiming in.
The videos also satirize how digital services slowly degrade over time. In one scene, the Enshittificator tells an employee, “The 1,000 pictures of your deceased mother are mine, and you’re going to pay for them.” It’s a direct nod to Google Photos’ 2021 policy shift, which ended free unlimited storage and capped free accounts at 15GB, requiring users to get a subscription to keep already uploaded photos on the platform.
Another scene takes a jab at automakers who sell you basic functionality as an add-on subscription service.
“I don’t have any more money. You have me in the palm of your hand,” said the Enshittificator in a fake presentation about selling cars. “You can crush me. So what do you do? Updates. Radio? Premium feature. Heating? Premium feature. Now I have a shitty car, and I can’t afford a new one, but what I can afford is a small monthly payment!”
This is a reference to BMW’s controversial microtransaction model, where it tried to make heated seats and other in-car features part of a subscription plan. While intense consumer backlash forced the German automaker to walk back some of the “add-ons,” several features remain behind a paywall. Other brands have followed suit — Hyundai’s BlueLink and Kia Connect require paid plans to use remote start. For a period, both manufacturers even omitted the remote-start button from the physical key fob, completely blocking owners from using the feature for free.
Can it be fixed?
It’s important, though a little depressing, to imagine how much better life would be if companies actually invested money into making their products better, safer and longer-lasting — and not just more profitable for them.
In its Breaking Free: Pathways to a Fair Technological Future report, the Norwegian Consumer Council argues that major tech business models “are often fundamentally incompatible with consumer and human rights.” To dismantle the “walled gardens run by Big Tech feudalists” and end dependence on Big Tech, the nonprofit is pushing for policy reforms built around a three-pronged strategy based on democratic values and principles of openness.
The first is interoperability, which would force platforms to interface with one another. This is already taking shape under the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required Apple to allow third-party app stores and mandated Meta to support external chats in WhatsApp,
Next comes portability, which would allow users to move their contacts, content, photos and anything else to rival services. A subscriber fed up with Spotify adding AI features, for instance, would be able to switch to YouTube Music or Apple Music without losing their saved playlists, thereby eliminating platform lock-in.
Finally, and arguably the most difficult to implement, is decentralization of social media, which could shift social media away from single-entity corporate control toward open networks like the Fediverse (which powers platforms such as Mastodon). Though still evolving as protocols develop, decentralization enhances interoperability, making cross-network movement frictionless.
Reining in Big Tech remains an uphill battle, but in the meantime, the campaign offers a hilarious — and painfully accurate — look at the modern digital hellscape.
“The true mark of success for a project like this is when other people pick it up and run with it,” Doctorow said.
results.summary:
The Norwegian Consumer Council has launched a satirical video campaign featuring the character Enshittificator to highlight how corporations deliberately degrade digital products and services to maximize short-term profits.

### Key Points
- The campaign, titled "Breaking Free," uses dark humor to critique planned obsolescence, subscription-based features, and the removal of essential product functionality.
- Author Cory Doctorow, who popularized the term "enshittification" in 2022, collaborated with the nonprofit to help expose corporate practices that prioritize revenue over consumer rights.
- The videos reference real-world examples, including Google Photos' storage caps, BMW’s subscription-based heated seats, and Apple’s "batterygate" settlement.
- The Norwegian Consumer Council advocates for policy reforms centered on interoperability, data portability, and the decentralization of social media to reduce Big Tech's market power.
- Legislative efforts like the EU’s Digital Markets Act are cited as necessary steps to force platforms to support third-party integration and open competition.

### Why it Matters
This campaign highlights a growing consumer movement against business models that prioritize corporate lock-in and planned obsolescence over product quality and longevity. By framing these practices as systemic issues rather than isolated incidents, the initiative pressures regulators to adopt policies that protect consumer autonomy in an increasingly digital economy.

results.title: Kraken Users Can Register For Ōura IPO Access Through xStocks
results.author: Bitcoinist Editorial Team
results.content:
- Payward Services has opened non-binding indications of interest for Ōura’s expected IPO through the xStocks ecosystem.
- Eligible Kraken users and customers of xStocks Alliance partners in more than 110 countries can register interest before the Nasdaq listing.
- On listing day, Payward says Ōura exposure is expected to become available as the tokenized ŌURAx product, subject to eligibility and the IPO proceeding.
**ID:** B25-06
**Site:** Bitcoinist
**Status:** READY
**Author:** Bitcoinist Editorial Team
**Focus Keyword:** Oura
**Image Keyword:** Tokenization
**Category:** Technology
**Tags:** Oura, Kraken, xStocks, IPO, Tokenization
**Primary Source:** https://www.businesswire.com/
The Pre-IPO Step Is An Indication Of Interest
Eligible users can register a non-binding indication of interest ahead of Ōura’s planned Nasdaq listing.
That wording is important.
Registering does not guarantee an allocation, and users are not buying Ōura shares simply by submitting interest through Kraken or another xStocks Alliance platform.
If the IPO proceeds, Payward says Ōura will become the fourth company to move through its IPO Access pipeline this year.
The previous offerings covered SpaceX, Bending Spoons and Jersey Mike’s.
Eligible users in more than 110 countries can participate through Kraken and other supported xStocks partners.
The Tokenized Product Comes After The Listing
Payward says Ōura will be tokenized as ŌURAx on listing day.
That would turn the newly public stock into an xStocks product designed for round-the-clock blockchain-based trading.
The model extends what crypto exchanges have been doing with existing public stocks into the IPO process itself.
Instead of waiting for shares to begin trading and then creating tokenized exposure later, Payward is trying to connect the pre-IPO allocation process directly with the tokenized secondary market.
There are still several layers of eligibility and regulation involved.
An xStock is not the same thing as directly holding a conventional brokerage share, and tokenized equities are unavailable in a number of jurisdictions.
The pre-IPO indication is also explicitly non-binding.
Still, the product shows how quickly the line between crypto exchanges and conventional brokerage infrastructure is disappearing.
Kraken increasingly wants users to access crypto, tokenized stocks and now IPO-linked products through the same broader ecosystem.
If Ōura completes its listing as planned, the transition from private-company exposure to a tokenized public-market instrument could happen almost immediately.
*This article was written by the News Desk and edited by [Samuel Rae](https://bitcoinist.com/author/samuelrae/).*

results.title: I wasn't sure about Googlebooks, but after playing with two Snapdragon-powered laptops, I'm actually considering switching
results.author: derrek.lee@futurenet.com (Derrek Lee) , Derrek Lee
results.content:
Qualcomm provided travel and lodging to Snapdragon Summit. There was no additional compensation, and Qualcomm did not have any input on this article prior to publication.
Earlier this year, Google introduced what had long been rumored: Android on your laptop. Googlebooks seem like a natural evolution of Chromebooks, and I got to spend some time with some of the first models at Qualcomm's Snapdragon Summit.
I expected it wouldn't be very different from Chromebooks, and that's... kind of true. Googlebooks aim to take the best parts of ChromeOS and Android and merge them into a very capable computing OS that can take advantage of AI and better connect to your smartphone.
I never quite liked Chromebooks, but I find myself quite compelled by the prospect of Googlebooks, even if the barrier to entry feels a bit high right now.
Not the Chromebook you remember
One major way the new Googlebooks differ from Chromebooks is their price. Chromebooks are compelling because they are available at very low price points, which benefits schools and other institutions with limited budgets. However, Chromebooks in their current form are pushing for a more premium experience, with the cheapest laptop costing $899.
That's still cheaper than most lower-end MacBooks, but prices can easily hit over $1,000, depending on the model and configuration. I was told this is because it's much easier to start at the higher end and work your way down than to start low and work your way up.
It's clear that Google wants to ensure that Googlebooks are seen as a premium computing experience before bringing cheaper options that will eventually supplant Chromebooks.
It's easy to see this in the hardware available. At Snapdragon Summit, I got to play with two Snapdragon X Elite-powered Googlebooks, the HP Googlebook 14 ($1,299) and Dell XPS Googlebook ($999). They feature exceptional hardware that looks and feels premium, something I never quite got from the Chromebooks I've used (though I know higher-end models exist).
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
The HP has a larger 14-inch OLED display that looks phenomenal, with a sharp resolution and deep blacks for more vibrant images. It also has comfortable keys and a large trackpad. Meanwhile, the Dell XPS has a smaller LCD panel with thin bezels and a matte finish to reduce reflections. Its aluminum build reminds me a bit of a MacBook, which speaks to how light and premium it feels in hand.
Both laptops share similar specs, including 16GB of RAM and 512GB of internal storage. They also feature built-in fingerprint sensors and the distinctive Glowbar, which offers functions like displaying battery life, Gemini interactions, and more. There's also a hidden easter egg that unlocks more controls, but I was told users have to find it themselves.
I'm not sure why Google is hiding this Glowbar control panel, since it feels like an essential or even fun part of the experience. Fortunately, Google plans to expand Glow Bar functionality, but for now it's a bit limited, just like HiLight on the Pixel 11 Pro.
Many UI elements also just feel very familiar. The quick settings panel feels very Pixel and sits in the top-right corner. The Settings app also looks like it came straight out of a Pixel Tablet, so anyone coming from an Android phone should feel at home.
You can also pin widgets to the home screen for glanceable info and create app folders, just like on an Android phone.
All about AI
What will further help Googlebooks shake the Chromebook perception is its capabilities. Thanks to more powerful chipsets like the Snapdragon X Elite, as well as Android being the foundation for the Googlebook OS, these devices are more capable than Chromebooks in a few areas, and much of that has to do with AI capabilities.
Googlebook really shines in its ability to perform more AI functions you'd normally find on an Android smartphone. One example I saw during my hands-on was Rambler, which lets users dictate notes, emails, and documents using natural language. The AI automatically filters out "ums" and even accounts for moments when you seem to change your mind about something you said.
What's neat is that Googlebooks come with a dedicated Rambler key, so you can easily access this with a tap.
One feature I think I'll get plenty of mileage out of is the Magic Pointer. It almost feels like a desktop Circle to Search: you can activate it by wiggling the pointer a bit, and it will prompt you to click an item on your screen you want to know more about. You can ask about one thing or add multiple items, and a Gemini dialogue opens in a side panel.
It feels like a natural evolution of the cursor, giving you easy access to Gemini when you need it. And speaking of Gemini, there's also Gemini Live, with a neat little circular UI similar to what you find on an Android phone, plus proactive intelligence and automation features, so you can have your computer complete tasks for you, just like on your phone.
And remember when I mentioned widgets? Well, you can use AI to create your own widget, and you can be as specific as you want. When demoing this feature, the widget creator was given a very specific, long-winded instruction to create a widget that would display the 49ers' points scored, comparisons with rival teams, and Brock Purdy's passing yards, all in a purple and neon-colored widget. And within less than a minute, it appeared on the desktop.
I can see this being a very useful feature for people who like to use their desktops like notepads. I also can't help but think of Windows 8 and its Tile interface, which were essentially dynamic "widgets" that filled your screen, although this feels more functional and a bit less jarring.
Finally, because Googlebooks run on the Android foundation, it's easy to download pretty much any app or game from the Play Store. You can also easily connect your phone to your Googlebook, search through your phone's app drawer, and cast apps directly to your desktop.
I didn't get to see this in action, but this sounds like an evolution of Phone Hub on Chromebooks. It also reminds me of Motorola's Smart Connect, which can do the same, though a native experience should be more useful.
For example, Continue On is a Handoff-like feature that lets you start one task on your phone and continue it on your laptop. And by connecting your phone to a Googlebook, you can easily swap files between devices without needing Quick Share or a physical connection.
A promising start
I didn't get to spend much time with the Googlebooks, and this is only a small selection of devices, with other options powered by Intel and even MediaTek chips. Still, it's a promising start for Google's computing ambitions, and I can't wait to see where the company takes it, especially as it moves down in price point.
We'll still have Chromebooks for a while, and some may even be able to update to Googlebook OS at some point in the future. While Google is working with developers to better optimize games for these larger screens, you shouldn't expect native PC-like AAA games on Googlebook, though you can still use GeForce NOW to stream games to your device.
So, Googlebook may not be for everyone, but it feels like a viable option for Android users who need to stay productive on the go when a tablet won't suffice, and it could also be a go-to option for students.
I was never a fan of Chromebooks, but I will admit that even I'm intrigued by Googlebooks, and I'm seriously considering switching from Windows.
Derrek is the managing editor of Android Central, helping to guide the site's editorial content and direction to reach and resonate with readers, old and new, who are just as passionate about tech as we are. He's been obsessed with mobile technology since he was 12, when he discovered the Nokia N90, and his love of flip phones and new form factors continues to this day. As a fitness enthusiast, he has always been curious about the intersection of tech and fitness. When he's not working, he's probably working out.

results.title: Top Stories: Apple Leaks, Siri AI Settlement, and More
results.author: MacRumors Staff
results.content:
The Apple rumor mill never stops, and this week MacRumors was able to break the news of details on several upcoming products.
We're also still learning more about the just-released iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max plus the upcoming iPhone Duo, while this week saw the debut of new Beats 360 headphones and the start of claim acceptance for the class action lawsuit over Siri AI delays, so read on below for all of the details on these stories and more!
Top Stories
iPad Mini With A20 Pro, New HomePod Mini Colors, and New Apple TV 4K All Just Leaked
MacRumors this week leaked the next iPad mini, HomePod mini, and Apple TV 4K models, all of which are likely to be announced this October as part of another wave of product launches including an all-new operating system to accompany some of the new hardware.
The most notable iPad mini details revealed in the leaks include an A20 Pro chip, a new speaker design, and a landscape front camera, while images have revealed that the next HomePod mini will be available in new colors like green and pink. There is also evidence of an upcoming "Apple TV 4K (4th generation)" model, so it appears that a new Apple TV is finally coming soon after a four-year wait.
A separate Apple code leak has confirmed some rumored details for the 12th-generation iPad, although we're not expecting that to launch until early next year.
Siri AI Settlement Website Now Live: Apple to Pay Some iPhone Owners
In May, Apple agreed to pay $250 million to settle a U.S. class action lawsuit over Siri AI's delayed launch, and the settlement website is now live.
Apple will pay an estimated $25 per eligible iPhone to eligible customers, who can submit a claim via the settlement website between September 21 and December 21 of this year. The exact payment may be higher or lower than $25 depending on the total number of valid claims submitted and other factors, with the maximum amount set at $95.
Apple denies all of the allegations made in the lawsuit, but agreed to the settlement to avoid the costs and risks of a trial.
iPhone 18 Pro Max Requires 'Prepare to Ship' Battery Drain Before Shipping
The iPhone 18 Pro Max has a single-cell battery capacity over 20 watt-hours, which means there are additional shipping requirements. If an iPhone 18 Pro Max needs to be shipped somewhere, its maximum battery capacity has to be limited through firmware.
According to Apple, the iPhone 18 Pro Max uses an "innovative battery-firmware solution" that limits battery capacity to below 20Wh between when the iPhone is manufactured and its delivery to a customer. Activating the iPhone removes the limit to make the battery's full charging capacity available.
Customers who need to ship the iPhone 18 Pro Max for repair, trade-in, or other purposes have to use a new Prepare to Ship feature. Prepare to Ship discharges the battery to below 20Wh and sets a charge limit so the iPhone stays below the threshold during the shipping process.
Apple Exec Says 'Hold Us Accountable' on iPhone Duo Crease
Apple hardware engineering VP Tom Marieb recently spoke with TechRadar and shared some candid thoughts about Apple's upcoming iPhone Duo.
The iPhone Duo uses a matte nano-texture display, which is meant to cut down on glare and minimize the visibility of the crease. When asked if the iPhone Duo's crease would be more visible over time, as that's what tends to happen on other foldables, Marieb said the nano-texture display would help. He asked people to hold the company "accountable" on crease visibility.
Marieb also discussed the Duo's innovative hinge, the use of Ceramic Shield 2 on the front display, and more.
Beats 360 Deliver Customizability and a Revamped Over-Ear Headphone Design
After months of teases and leaks, Apple's Beats brand officially announced its new Beats 360 headphone this week. Priced at $349.99, Beats 360 represents a rethinking of the Beats over-ear headphone design, with an emphasis on sound quality, comfort, and customizability.
Beats 360 is not a replacement for the brand's Studio Pro over-ear headphone, as the Studio Pro will remain part of the Beats lineup at a reduced price point of $299.99, down from the previous $349.99. Compared to Studio Pro, Beats 360 features a completely new acoustic architecture that delivers up to 1.75× more active noise cancellation and a 12dB increase in output while maintaining clarity across all frequencies with low distortion.
Swappable ear and headband cushions let you customize your look by mixing and matching colors and materials, with Beats offering extra cushion kits at heavily discounted prices as part of a launch promo.
iPhone 20 Pro Display Sizes Leak Ahead of 2027 Launch
Apple's 20th-anniversary iPhone lineup coming next year could feature slightly larger displays than the iPhone 18 Pro models, if a recent leak shared on Weibo is accurate.
Prolific Chinese leaker Digital Chat Station claims that early iPhone 20 Pro display specifications include a 6.41-inch screen with a resolution of approximately 2,686 × 1,236 pixels, while the iPhone 20 Pro Max is said to have a 6.96-inch display with a resolution of around 2,912 × 1,340 pixels.
For comparison, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max feature 6.27 inches (rounded to 6.3 inches) and 6.86 inches (rounded to 6.9 inches) respectively. Meanwhile, the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max resolutions are 2,622 × 1,206 pixels and 2,868 × 1,320 pixels, respectively.
MacRumors Newsletter
Each week, we publish an email newsletter like this highlighting the top Apple stories, making it a great way to get a bite-sized recap of the week hitting all of the major topics we've covered and tying together related stories for a big-picture view.
So if you want to have top stories like the above recap delivered to your email inbox each week, subscribe to our newsletter!

results.title: GitHub Actions re-enabled with Mini Shai-Hulud payload still active
results.author: Bill Toulas
results.content:
Two third-party GitHub Actions previously compromised in a Mini Shai-Hulud campaign were re-enabled by their maintainer and remained accessible for more than a week despite still pointing to malicious code.
After being compromised on May 18, the GitHub security team removed actions-cool/issues-helper and actions-cool/maintain-one-comment, preventing any downstream workflow from downloading malware.
According to researchers at application security company Socket, starting September 16 and up to September 25, the two actions became active again with the same release tags, causing workflows referencing their actions to download and execute the old payload.
The Mini Shai-Hulud supply-chain attack in May affected 323 packages and 639 package versions on the Node Package Manager (npm) index, infecting them with malware that targets developers’ tokens, credentials, and CI/CD secrets.
Socket researchers found that last Wednesday the release tags for actions-cool/issues-helper and actions-cool/maintain-one-comment resolved to a commit containing the obfuscated payload inside the ‘index.js’ file.
“On September 16, 2026, both repositories became accessible again. Their release tags were not cleaned up first," Socket explained.
"They still point to the malicious content introduced on May 18, so any workflow that references either action by a version tag resumed downloading and executing the payload on its next run.”
It is unclear exactly why these repositories were re-enabled without proper cleaning occurring first.
Socket says that GitHub’s dependency graph lists about 15,000 repositories depending on ‘issues-helper,’ though this does not mean all of them were compromised.
The researchers note that they have not yet established how many dependents reference either action by mutable tag instead of a pinned commit.
However, they explained that the impacted actions are those running almost daily, as they support issue-housekeeping needs.
On September 25, Socket found that both actions were disabled again on GitHub, leading workflows that reference them to fail instead of running the payload.
Socket recommends finding references to both actions, removing them or pinning a verified clean commit, reviewing runs since September 16, and rotating secrets accessible to workflows that ran an affected tag.
Potentially impacted developers should look for references to both actions and remove them or pin a verified clean commit.
The exposure started on September 16 between 11:09 and 18:16 GMT+2.
Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed.
Save your seat

Two compromised GitHub Actions linked to the Mini Shai-Hulud supply-chain attack were inadvertently re-enabled by their maintainer, exposing thousands of downstream repositories to malicious code for over a week.

### Key Points
- Security researchers at Socket discovered that two GitHub Actions, actions-cool/issues-helper and actions-cool/maintain-one-comment, were re-enabled on September 16.
- The re-enabled actions still pointed to malicious payloads from a May 18 supply-chain attack, which targeted developer credentials and CI/CD secrets.
- Approximately 15,000 repositories depend on the affected actions, which were finally disabled again by GitHub on September 25.
- The original Mini Shai-Hulud campaign compromised 323 packages and 639 versions on the npm registry.
- Socket recommends that developers rotate potentially exposed secrets and pin dependencies to verified, clean commits to prevent future unauthorized code execution.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the significant risks associated with using mutable tags in software supply chains, as automated workflows can silently pull malicious updates without developer intervention. Organizations must implement stricter dependency management practices to ensure that compromised third-party tools do not provide attackers with persistent access to sensitive CI/CD environments.

results.title: Novel attack slashes computing power needed to crack textbook RSA cryptography
results.author: editors@tomshardware.com (Bruno Ferreira) , Bruno Ferreira
results.content:
Factoring attacks against the RSA algorithm were generally considered infeasible, but that may change dramatically if the findings in a paper from UC San Diego (California) and Inria Nancy (France) prove correct after peer review. The paper outlines a new attack that breaks RSA in record time. That's concerning because RSA-based encryption was in use for quite some time, and although it's been generally deprecated in favor of ECC and post-quantum algorithms, it's still employed today in a substantial portion of services.
Assuming the research holds up and the attack conditions are met, the number of necessary operations for cracking an RSA-encrypted key (and thus, inspecting network traffic encrypted with it) drops dramatically. (From 280, 2112, 2128, and 2144 down to 265, 290, 2105, and 2119 — for 1024, 2048, 3072-, and 4096-bit key lengths, respectively.)
Even for the 1024-bit keys, performing 265 calculations is still a lot, but it starts getting into the range where it's feasible for an entity with large resources at their disposal, like a number of state actors. Crucially, the paper indicates that the algorithms the team used are far from optimized and could hypothetically be significantly sped up after optimization passes, potentially with the help of AI tools and by leveraging GPUs for the task.
The attack only works against the textbook (or "raw") variant of RSA, which isn't widely used for commonplace computing like website certificates and remote access, but is nevertheless present in services like Cloudflare Privacy Pass, iCloud Private Relay, and Private Cloud Compute. Equipment and services using PKCS #11, like many smart cards, USB security tokens, code-signing pipelines, hardware security (HSM) and trusted platform (TPM) modules also use this variation. But fulfilling the attack conditions is much easier said than done.
In order to reach a point where an attacker can decipher data, they first must perform an exceedingly high number of queries against the key they're attacking, collecting enough data points from the key's oracle. In practical terms, this often means repeatedly poking a live server that's using that key to encrypt traffic, billions of times over, though it can also be done against a standalone hardware device.
In the practical context of an encryption algorithm, an oracle takes a number in, runs it through a computation involving a private key, and spits it back out, without revealing its key. The textbook variant of RSA under attack here lets the oracle be queried with any number, thus allowing the attacker to collect enough data points to perform the mathematical wizardry described in the paper. They can then proceed to throw a lot of computing power to ultimately inspect whichever traffic they captured that was using that same encryption key.
As network administrators have certainly figured out by now, running billions of queries against a live service is almost guaranteed to earn them an IP ban, among other measures. It's a reasonable assumption that entities like Cloudflare and Apple have those kinds of controls in place. Still, not everyone does, especially in the case of key management services that aren't closely monitored, including hardware-based ones. The scientists worked their magic on Thales Luna HSMs, in both hardware and online service form.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Although the bar for a practical application of this attack remains quite high, the key finding is that it may be significantly lowered. This opens the possibility that oracle data collected today may be used to decrypt saved traffic in a matter of weeks or months, especially in the near future as hardware advances. It's also possible that other scientists can take this idea and expand on it, finding additional flaws.

Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

### Key Points

- The attack specifically targets the "textbook" or "raw" variant of RSA, which is utilized in services like Cloudflare Privacy Pass, Apple iCloud Private Relay, and various hardware security modules.
